author: William Saville
reader_character: Jasper — adult first-person protagonist, externally they/them
title: Permission for Privacy
subtitle: Lanternweald — sixth expansion pass
content:
The chalkboard in Lanternwell Square had acquired a new column.

It stood beside the bakery menu under the heading *Who's with Jasper?* Someone had drawn six little hearts and written the names of people I cared about, with blank spaces for dates and guesses.

I stared until the letters stopped making sense.

Mara came out carrying a tray of rolls. She saw the board and went still.

"That's not mine."

"I know."

"I was going to wipe it off, but I thought you should decide whether you wanted to see it first."

I swallowed. I was furious with the person who'd written it, but I was also strangely ashamed. The chalkboard made my life look like a game people could follow, score, and argue about over breakfast.

"Would you give me the cloth?" I asked.

Mara handed it over.

I wiped the names away.

Behind me someone said, "Oh. I thought it was just a joke."

I turned. A man I recognized from the market stood holding a basket of apples. He looked embarrassed rather than cruel.

"Whose joke?" I asked.

"People were talking. You and Maui, and the others. We wondered how it all worked."

"Then you could have asked me a question that didn't require exposing six people's private lives."

He shifted the basket. "I didn't think anyone would mind."

"You didn't ask them."

I heard my voice grow sharper. I wanted to make him feel exactly as small as the board had made me feel. I was not proud of that.

Maui arrived before I could say anything else. He looked at the damp board, then at my face.

"What happened?"

I told him.

His jaw tightened. For a moment I saw the old Maui, ready to turn the whole square into a battlefield because someone had embarrassed a person he loved.

He looked at me. "What do you want?"

"Not a speech from you," I said quickly. "Please."

He breathed in, then out. "All right."

I asked Neri for five minutes at the community notice board. A few people gathered, including several who had seen the chalkboard before it was erased. I kept the account plain.

"I'm ethically non-monogamous," I said. "I prefer polyamory. The people in my relationships know that. They each make their own choices, and some of those choices are private."

A woman raised her hand. "So you don't have to tell everyone?"

"No. Neither do you."

"What about fairness?"

"Fairness means honesty with the people affected, respecting consent, and keeping the commitments we actually make. It doesn't mean putting everyone's schedule on a public board."

Someone asked whether my partners liked each other.

"That's their business," I said. "Some have worked together. Some want space. None of them owes the square a performance."

The man with the apples had stayed near the edge of the crowd. He looked down at his basket.

I could have called him out by name.

I didn't.

Instead I asked the council to put a privacy rule beside the public festival guidelines: notice boards were for community business, not speculation about residents' romantic lives. Mara added a second rule about not writing personal contact information without permission.

Neri approved the notice.

It wasn't a law against gossip. People would still talk. But it established a boundary the community could enforce in the spaces it maintained.

Later, I found Maui at Tideglass repairing a lantern hook.

"Are you angry?" I asked.

"Yes."

"At me?"

"At the board."

I leaned against the post. "You didn't say much."

"You asked me not to."

"Was that difficult?"

"Extremely. I had three speeches ready."

I laughed despite myself.

He put down the hook.

"Did you mean what you said about us not needing to explain everything?"

"Yes."

"Because sometimes I don't want to know what you and Severus talk about, or how Iroh says goodnight. Sometimes I do want to know when your plans affect ours. And sometimes I worry that wanting that makes me selfish."

I took his hand.

"You can ask. I can decide what belongs to me to share. If it belongs to someone else too, I ask them first."

He frowned.

"What about kisses?"

"Those are ours when they're between us. We can talk about them if we both want. They're not the village's property."

He smiled slowly.

"Good."

The sunset lit the signal post in amber. I could hear Lio arguing with Fen about a skiff measurement and the bakery bell sounding faintly from the square. There was a whole life around us, full of people who deserved to have some parts remain their own.

Maui stepped closer.

"May I kiss you somewhere nobody's taking notes?"

"Yes."

We went home by the upper path, laughing when the wind tried to steal his cloak. At the door he kissed me, then again after I pulled him closer. The rest of the evening was private, the door closed because we had chosen it.

The next morning the chalkboard held the day's bread prices and the tide warning, nothing else.

There were six hearts still faintly visible beneath the damp surface.

I didn't erase them again.

The boundary was the important part. The trace of somebody's mistake could stay without deciding what happened next.
